passages.happening:
“Surely there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined. Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore” (verses 1-2).

Man puts an end to darkness and probes the farthest depths for ore. Far from where anyone lives, he cuts a shaft, ‘in places forgotten by the foot of man. Far from men he dangles and sways’ (verse 4). Bread grows from the surface of the earth, but below it is turned over as by fire.

“No bird of prey knows that path; no falcon’s eye has seen it. Proud beasts have never trodden it; no lion has ever prowled over it” (verses 7-8). The miner strikes the flint, overturns mountains at their roots, cuts channels in the rock and dams the streams ‘to bring what is hidden to light’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The debate with the friends is over. It ended without agreement, the friends silenced and Job still protesting. This chapter pauses the drama with a calm poem, very different in tone from the heated speeches around it.

It begins with mining, one of the most advanced skills of the ancient world. Miners dug shafts and tunnels deep into the earth, working by lamplight in total darkness, sometimes lowered on ropes. Copper mining and smelting in the Arabah, south of the Dead Sea, is well attested by archaeology, at sites such as Timna and Faynan. Ancient readers knew that mining was dangerous and difficult, and that it reached places no animal had ever gone.

The point of the first part is admiration. Human beings can find almost anything hidden in the earth.
passages.asks: The poem admires what people can dig out of the earth. Ask what you have worked hardest to find or to gain. And ask whether it is the thing you most need.

passages.happening:
“But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell? No man can know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living” (verses 12-13). The deep says it is not there, and the sea says it is not with it.

It cannot be bought with gold or weighed out in silver. ‘It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire’ (verse 16). Crystal, coral and quartz are not worth mentioning; ‘the price of wisdom is beyond rubies’ (verse 18). Topaz from Cush cannot compare.

“From where then does wisdom come, and where does understanding dwell? It is hidden from the eyes of every living thing and concealed from the birds of the air” (verses 20-21). Even Abaddon and Death have heard only a rumor of it.
passages.hearers:
The poem is built around a refrain, asked twice, in verses 12 and 20, like the chorus of a song: where can wisdom be found?

Wisdom in the ancient world was a prized possession, sought by kings and taught in schools. It covered practical skill, good judgment and an understanding of how the world works and how to live well in it. The question where wisdom is found is really a question about the deepest meaning of the world. Job's friends thought they had it. The poem says it lies beyond anyone's reach.

The precious things listed were the most valuable in that economy. Ophir was famous for its gold, and Cush, south of Egypt, for gold and rare goods. The identity of several of the stones is uncertain, and translations vary.

The deep, the sea, Abaddon and Death are given voices. They were the most remote places in the ancient picture of the world. If even they have only heard a rumor of wisdom, no living creature can find it.
passages.later: Proverbs uses the same comparison: “For wisdom is more precious than rubies, and nothing you desire compares with her” (Proverbs 8:11).
passages.asks: The poem says wisdom cannot be bought. Ask where you look for wisdom when life does not make sense. And ask whether you have treated wisdom as something to own rather than something to receive.

passages.t: The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom
passages.happening:
“But God understands its way, and He knows its place. For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens” (verses 23-24).

When God fixed the weight of the wind and measured out the waters, when he set a limit for the rain and a path for the thunderbolt, ‘then He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out’ (verse 27).

And he said to man that ‘the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The answer to the refrain: God alone knows the way to wisdom, because he established it when he ordered the world. The world is built by wisdom, which is why it is ordered and can be understood, even when its deepest meaning is hidden.

The last verse turns from the cosmic to the personal. What human beings cannot find, God gives. They receive wisdom not by discovering it but by fearing God and turning from evil, living rightly with the one who knows. The fear of the Lord is not terror but reverent trust and obedience. The word for Lord here is Adonai, found only here in Job in the standard Hebrew text.

The last line brings the book back to its first verse, where Job is described as a man ‘fearing God and shunning evil’ (1:1).
passages.later: The same saying stands at the start of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:7) and again here: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding” (Proverbs 9:10).
passages.hard:
Who speaks this poem, and why does it stand here?

The chapter follows straight on from Job's speech in chapter 27 with no new introduction, so in the text as it stands Job is the speaker. But its tone is strikingly different from his speeches before and after: calm and reflective rather than anguished. If Job already knew that wisdom is found in fearing God, it is hard to explain why he goes back to protest in chapters 29 to 31.

For these reasons many interpreters think the poem is an interlude spoken by the book's narrator, commenting on the failed debate and preparing for what follows. Others argue that Job does speak it, and that it is a moment of calm insight in the middle of his struggle which he does not yet know how to live out. A third view sees it as a deliberate preview of God's speeches, showing the reader what Job will learn. These notes take no side.

On any view, the poem stands near the center of the book and names its deepest theme: wisdom is found not by solving the mystery of suffering but by fearing God in the middle of it.
passages.asks: The poem says that wisdom is to fear God and turn from evil. Ask what that would look like in the hardest thing you are facing now. And ask whether you have been trying to understand everything before you trust him.
